scenes.narration: A P L C never reacts to a wire directly. Every scan, it does three things, in order. First, it reads every input, all at once, into memory. We call that the input image. Second, it solves your rungs, top to bottom, using that frozen snapshot. Third, it writes every output, all at once, from memory. That is the output image. Then it does it all again, often many times a second.
caption: A PLC never reacts to a wire directly. Every scan does three things, in order.
First: read every input, all at once, into the input image.
Second: solve your rungs, top to bottom, using that frozen snapshot.
Third: write every output, all at once, the output image. Then it does it all again.

scenes.narration: Here is why the order inside step two matters. This program has three rungs, on purpose written in an order that catches people out. Rung one reads the run lamp and drives the motor. Rung two reads Start and drives the run lamp. See the problem. Rung one runs first, so it only ever sees what the run lamp was at the start of this scan, not what rung two is about to write.
caption: Here's why the order inside step two matters.
Three rungs, written on purpose in an order that catches people out.
Rung 1 reads the run lamp and drives the motor. Rung 2 reads Start and drives the run lamp.
Rung 1 runs first, so it only sees what the run lamp was at the START of this scan.

scenes.narration: Let's slow it right down and watch. I am holding Start in. Step one scan. Rung two just copied Start into the run lamp, so the lamp is on. But rung one already ran this scan, before the lamp changed, so the motor is still off. Step the scan again. Now rung one sees the run lamp as it was at the end of last scan, true, so the motor finally turns on. One whole scan late, just because of rung order.

scenes.narration: Rung three has no such trap. It is the simplest program there is, one input straight to one output, in the same scan. AUX drives the beacon, with no delay at all. Most of your programs will look like this. The one scan delay only bites when a later rung's output feeds an earlier rung's input, in the same scan.

For your lab, you will be given an input sequence, and you need to predict the output after each scan. Walk through it rung by rung, exactly like we just did.
